title: Interval conventions in binary search
summary: Whether right-boundary pointer j is included in the search interval directly determines the initial value of j, the loop termination condition, and how j is updated when narrowing leftward.
context: An illustrative ascending array contains n = 10 elements indexed from 0 to 9; pointers i and j mark the left and right boundaries of the current search interval, and m denotes the current midpoint index. Bar heights only indicate monotonic increase without labeling specific element values.
description: In both diagrams, a blue dashed box encloses all ten elements. On the left, for the “closed interval [i, j],” right pointer j points to the last bar and includes that position; on the right, for the “half-open interval [i, j)” (left-closed, right-open), j points just past the rightmost bar and excludes that position. Substituting n = 10 into the initialization formulas gives j = 9 on the left and j = 10 on the right.

When i = j, the closed interval still contains one element to check, whereas the half-open interval is already empty. When narrowing leftward, the right endpoint of a closed interval is included, so j = m - 1 is used to exclude m; the right endpoint of a half-open interval is already excluded, so j = m is assigned directly. The table below lists the four rules shown in the figure and adds the corresponding while-loop condition opposite to each termination condition.
